claims.text: The as-synthesized baseline HfNbTaTiZr alloy is near-equiatomic, with approximately 20 at.% of each element.
Increasing the Hf percentage in HfNbTaTiZr will increase its yield strength.
Increasing the Hf percentage in HfNbTaTiZr will increase its hardness.
Increasing Hf content increases lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing Hf content may promote local chemical ordering.
Greater lattice distortion increases resistance to dislocation motion.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion produces greater mechanical strength and hardness.
A composition library can be prepared by increasing Hf in approximately 5 at.% increments while reducing one or more other constituents.
Room-temperature tensile testing can be used to measure the relationship between Hf concentration and yield strength.
Nanoindentation can be used to measure the relationship between Hf concentration and hardness.
XRD or TEM can be used to determine whether the varied compositions remain single phase.
Samples containing more Hf are predicted to have higher yield strength than the equiatomic baseline.
Samples containing more Hf are predicted to have higher hardness than the equiatomic baseline.
The mechanical enhancement may plateau or reverse if secondary phases form.
The proposed strengthening relationship is valid only while the alloy remains single phase and avoids pronounced segregation.
The equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has known mechanical properties reported in prior HEA studies.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts the hypothesis to single-phase alloys, and the predicted outcome permits plateauing or reversal after secondary phases form, yet the falsification rule suggests that observations involving secondary-phase formation could reject the hypothesis. Results outside the stated single-phase boundary therefore are not consistently treated.
